evidence_set: People planning to attend a ceremony with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD) were recruited by online advertisements to a study website; eligibility: aged 18 or over, good English, and the intention to take part in a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic. Survey links went out about a week before, one day after and 4 weeks after the indicated date, and the two main measures (the Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire and nine FAD-Plus free-will and fatalism items) were taken at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months. Baseline table: N = 819, age 44.4 ± 12.6 (not labelled; presumably mean ± SD), 359 women (43.8%) and 455 men (55.6%), United States 43.8%, United Kingdom 19.5%, master's degree 33.6% and doctorate or professional degree 20.5%, White 90.7%, median household income 9000 dollars a month. Trial: 59 patients with major depression who completed a double-blind randomized trial (30 given two 25 mg doses of psilocybin and 6 weeks of daily placebo, 29 given two 1 mg doses and daily escitalopram), with an adapted questionnaire at baseline and 6 weeks; registered as NCT03429075.

866 respondents are said to have completed the belief survey at different time points. The 13-item questionnaire (ten items written for the survey, three from earlier work) gave one factor of nine items, Non-physicalist Beliefs (Cronbach's alpha 0.86), loading positively on another realm that can be visited (0.790), a supernatural transition to such realms (0.740), a unifying principle beyond any material or scientific explanation (0.776), panpsychism (0.642), primacy of other realms (0.592), dualism (0.444) and the physical world as an illusion generated by consciousness or the mind (0.441), and negatively on materialism (−0.727) and naturalism (−0.598). The authors say the relation between items and philosophical positions could be contested, so the items are arguably best taken at face value.

Item means (with standard errors) at baseline lie on the agree side of neutral for ontological and supernatural transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism, primacy of other realms and dualism, and on the disagree side for materialism, naturalism and solipsism/idealism. Changes are marked as significant at 6 months (**) for ontological and supernatural transcendentalism, materialism (down), panpsychism and dualism, and at 4 weeks only (*) for non-naturalism and primacy of other realms; naturalism and solipsism/idealism carry no marker, although the legend lists solipsism/idealism among the items that shifted. The axis runs from Disagree to Agree without numbers, so item changes cannot be given in scale units.

Respondents whose remembered Mystical Experience Questionnaire score was at or above the median reported larger increases than those below it; in Figure 2 their 'before' ratings were similar, and their 'after' ratings differed meaningfully for every entity except other humans; the relation held with the score as a continuous variable after adjustment for eight demographic, psychedelic-use and other variables including psychological challenge (no model statistics in the main text; Supplementary Table 3, cited for the group comparison, not read; group sizes not given).

evidence_set: The authors call this the first study to show personality change in healthy adults after an experimentally manipulated discrete event and call for replication in larger groups with diverse baseline personalities; they compare the rise with the usual fall in Openness of about 1 T point per decade in normal ageing and with smaller rises after antidepressant treatment or intensive outpatient counselling, figures from other studies; and they write that differences in participants' motivation and preparation likely contributed to the different outcome of an earlier LSD study, and that it is possible that their regularly spiritually active participants are particularly sensitive to psilocybin's mystical-type effects, which predicted the Openness increases.

No factor of the NEO PI-R personality inventory, and neither the positive nor the negative affect scale of the PANAS-X, was differentially affected by psilocybin: the two order groups (15 given psilocybin first, 15 methylphenidate first) did not differ significantly at screening or 2 months after session 1, and the methylphenidate-first group showed no significant change from after session 1 to after session 2, its psilocybin session. No values are shown.

Three adults nominated by each participant, interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session (N = 26), rated a mean positive change in the participant's behaviour and attitudes of 2.42 (SEM 0.70) after psilocybin against -0.03 (SEM 0.68) after methylphenidate (p < 0.01), which the authors call a small but significant positive change. The paper does not relate these ratings to the personality scores.

Materials and methods › Community observer ratings of changes in participants' behavior and attitudes (p. 273); Table 4 and Results › Community observer ratings of changes in participants' and behavior and attitudes (heading as printed) (p. 278)

Of 36 enrolled (14 men), 30 were randomized to drug order (15 per order) and 6 to a decoy arm that had methylphenidate twice and then open-label psilocybin in a third session; the decoy arm's data were left out of the statistical analyses. MacLean et al. took 35 of these 36 into their analysis (one excluded for incomplete personality data) and describe every high-dose session as blinded, so their 35 would include at least five of the six open-label sessions (editors' inference).
Materials and methods › Participants and Study design (p. 269); Instructions to participants and monitors, last paragraph (p. 271: these six third sessions were the only unblinded sessions)

Openness change did not correlate with treatment response or differ between responders and non-responders, which the authors call consistent with Openness being orthogonal to anxiety or depression symptoms (while noting some findings of a moderate relation with wellbeing) and take as support for the change potentially being in addition to, rather than a direct effect of, improved mood, citing their own unpublished survey (data not shown). Against d values they computed from three antidepressant trials (five samples, 469 patients, 8 to 20 weeks), Neuroticism, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness changed similarly (−0.59, 0.04 and 0.18 there; −0.57, −0.01 and 0.27 here), while Openness (0.44 against 0.13) and Extraversion (0.72 against 0.32) changed more; they advise caution because follow-up times differ. From these data, they write, it is hard to infer that the changes, in particular in Neuroticism and Extraversion, are trait rather than state changes, though a change lasting 3 months might suggest more than a state artefact.

evidence_set: If inhibition between neighbouring orientation patches is weak, V1 behaves without intrinsic orientation tuning and, if the lateral interactions are still effective, non-contoured patterns (contrasting regions of light and dark) arise, corresponding to tunnels, funnels and spirals; if it is strong, contoured patterns (lattices of oriented edges) arise, corresponding to honeycombs, chequer-boards and cobwebs (elsewhere, pp. 303 and 312, the paper groups chequer-boards with the light-and-dark patterns). The Discussion says all but the square patterns are stable; the authors say hallucinations resembling square patterns exist and may be transitional forms.

The authors present the model as showing that common hallucinatory images can be generated by a biologically plausible architecture, with the instability presumed to occur, for example, shortly after hallucinogens act on brain-stem nuclei that control cortical excitability; the Discussion concludes that V1 circuits normally involved in detecting oriented edges and processing contours are also responsible for generating the form constants, a firmer wording than the abstract's 'interesting possibility'.

Restricting the solutions to doubly periodic patterns is standard but, the authors write, has as yet no formal justification, although they cite evidence from convecting fluids, chemical reaction-diffusion systems and neural-net simulations that such systems tend to form doubly periodic patterns. Many variants of the form constants have been described, some of which, the authors write, cannot be understood in terms of their simple model: a tunnel with reversed magnification (possibly involving circuits beyond V1, such as dorsal MSTd); a lattice-tunnel attributed to marijuana, more complicated than the simple form constants, for which they suggest a mismatch between a planform and the somewhat disordered cortical lattice and show a simulation (a hexagonal roll on a slightly incommensurate square lattice); and a complex image after LSD, which does not fit a form constant well and may involve two length-scales, beyond the scope of the model.

The authors offer a prediction for experimental testing: if V1 implements the double retinocortical map, cells tuned to the same relative angle should be preferentially connected, and orientation changes should be relatively large and detectable with optical imaging near the horizontal meridian. Separately, they cite reports (Siegel & Jarvik, 1975) that after LSD and similar drugs many people see a bright white light at the centre of the visual field that explodes into a hallucination in about 3 seconds, which they say corresponds to activity spreading across V1 at about 2.4 cm per second and present as an observed instance of a propagating-wave scenario consistent with their analysis. Neither is tested in the paper.
